Emerging strategies, including bispecific antibodies, immunotoxins, and senolytic elimination of GPNMB-high damaged cells, are expanding the therapeutic landscape. This review dissects the molecular mechanisms, pathological roles, and evolving clinical applications of GPNMB in cancer, highlighting current challenges and future directions for precision oncology.

title: Therapeutic resistance in cancer: lncRNAs as modulators and targets for cancer therapy.
abstract: Therapeutic resistance continues to be a significant challenge in cancer treatment, often leading to tumor recurrence, metastasis, and limited therapeutic efficacy despite advancements in chemotherapy and radiotherapy. This resistance arises from complex molecular mechanisms that are influenced by various factors, including genetic alterations, epigenetic modifications, and cellular signaling. Recently, lncRNAs, a subclass of non-coding RNAs, have gained prominence for their essential role in driving cancer progression and mediating resistance to therapy. The resistance phenotype is shaped by lncRNAs through the regulation of key signaling pathways, DNA repair mechanisms, and cellular survival processes. For example, lncRNAs such as HOTAIR and MALAT1 are involved in the regulation of PI3K/AKT, EMT, and DNA repair pathways, and influence cell proliferation, apoptosis, and metastasis. These findings underscore the potential of lncRNAs as therapeutic targets. Targeting lncRNA-mediated pathways offers a promising approach to overcome resistance and enhance the efficacy of existing therapies. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the molecular mechanisms by which lncRNAs mediate resistance in various cancers, such as gastric cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma. By focusing on the therapeutic potential of lncRNAs, we propose new avenues for overcoming resistance and improving treatment outcomes in cancer therapy.

title: Structural and molecular insights into Helicobacter pylori CagA-SHP2 complex: From pathogenic signaling to targeted therapeutic opportunities in gastric cancer.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global health burden, ranking as the fifth most common malignancy worldwide. Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is strongly implicated in gastric carcinogenesis and was classified as a Class 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1994. Among H. pylori virulence factors, cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA) plays a pivotal oncogenic role by modulating host signaling pathways through highly specialized molecular interactions utilizing the CagA multimerization (CM) and EPIYA motifs. Following translocation into gastric epithelial cells (GECs) via the type IV secretion system (T4SS), tyrosine phosphorylation at EPIYA motifs ensures aberrant interaction between CagA and the host Src homology 2 domain-containing phosphatase 2 (SHP2). This interaction represents a unique host-pathogen crosstalk mechanism that functionally mimics oncogenic PTPN11 gain-of-function mutations, resulting in sustained activation of MAPK/ERK and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) pathways, cytoskeletal reorganization, increased cellular motility, and the characteristic hummingbird phenotype. This review aims to summarize current knowledge on the structural and functional interplay between CagA and SHP2 and its role in gastric carcinogenesis, while broadly addressing how geographic diversity in CagA variants shapes the interaction and its consequences. It further discusses the broader oncogenic impact of CagA-driven signaling alterations, including emerging evidence for a hit-and-run oncogenic mechanism, and their relevance to disease progression and prevention strategies. The CagA-SHP2 axis emerges as a central pathogenic hub in H. pylori-associated gastric carcinogenesis and an attractive pharmacological target for the development of mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for the disease.

title: Validation of an AI‑Assisted Open‑Source software (CoreSlicer) for CT‑Based body composition analysis in locally advanced gastric Cancer: A Comparative study with SliceOmatic.
abstract: This study aimed to validate the agreement between CoreSlicer (AI-assisted segmentation with manual calibration) and SliceOmatic (manual segmentation) for CT-based body composition analysis in gastric cancer patients. This retrospective study included 261 patients with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma. Pre- and post-treatment L3-level CT images were analyzed using both software programs. Skeletal muscle area (SMA), visceral adipose tissue area (VAT), and subcutaneous adipose tissue area (SAT) were measured, and corresponding indices (SMI, SAI, VAI) were calculated. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen's kappa. Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to predict major pathological response (MPR), and model discrimination was compared using the area under the curve (AUC). Excellent agreement was observed for SMA (ICC: pre-treatment 0.997, post-treatment 0.997), SAT (ICC: 0.990, 0.990), and VAT (ICC: 0.964, 0.942). Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal bias for SMA and SAT, whereas VAT was systematically overestimated by CoreSlicer. Diagnostic agreement for muscle atrophy was excellent (kappa: 0.923). Both methods showed similar predictive performance for MPR (AUC = 0.675). CoreSlicer with manual calibration demonstrates excellent agreement with SliceOmatic for body composition measurements, supporting its use as a reliable alternative to manual segmentation in clinical practice.

title: DEK recruits KAT6A regulate H3K27ac/c-myc axis to drive enhanced glycolysis and immune escape in gastric cancer.
abstract: Increased glycolytic activity and immune evasion mechanisms in gastric cancer represent significant impediments to therapeutic advancements. In this study, KAT6A was strikingly upregulated in both gastric cancer tissues and cell lines and was significantly associated with malignant phenotypes and shorter survival periods. We have demonstrated that KAT6A upregulates acetylated histone levels, thereby increasing the transcriptional activity of genes, including HK2, PDL1, and CD47. This consequently promotes elevated glycolytic flux and facilitates immune evasion. Notably, for the first time, we discovered that DEK plays a crucial synergistic role in the activation of H3K27ac by KAT6A and that the knockout of DEK can rescue the related effects of overexpressing KAT6A. Moreover, knockdown of KAT6A and DEK suppressed malignant phenotypes in gastric cancer cells, including proliferation, invasion, and migration, while enhancing macrophage phagocytic function and CD8+ T-cell activity. Moreover, combined treatment with KAT6A inhibition and an anti-CD47 agent has excellent therapeutic efficacy. These findings reveal the regulatory mechanism through which KAT6A and DEK cooperate to regulate glycolysis levels and immune escape in gastric cancer and provide therapeutic targets and promising treatment strategies for tumor intervention.

title: B3GNT2 promotes gastric cancer metastasis by facilitating membrane trafficking of RYK via N-glycosylation.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is characterized by a high metastatic propensity, which constitutes the primary cause of poor patient prognosis. Receptor-like tyrosine kinase (RYK) is associated with GC metastasis, but its regulatory mechanism remains unclear. Primary and metastatic GC tissues, together with their matched adjacent non-tumor samples, were collected. GC cell models were established to systematically evaluate the driver role of RYK in GC metastasis. We further integrated clinical specimens, GC cell models, and a mouse model of GC liver metastasis, and combined immunohistochemistry, real-time quantitative PCR, Western blot, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, wound-healing assays, 3D sphere invasion assays, and co-immunoprecipitation to elucidate the biological functions and molecular mechanisms of RYK in GC metastasis. RYK expression was higher in both primary and metastatic tumor tissues than in adjacent normal tissues. Overexpression of RYK markedly enhanced the invasion and migration capacities of GC cells and induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition; blocking its membrane localization promptly attenuated this pro-metastatic effect. Mechanistically, β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 2 (B3GNT2) bound to RYK and catalyzed its N-glycosylation, thereby promoting RYK trafficking to the plasma membrane. In GC cell models and a liver-metastasis mouse model, GC cells overexpressing B3GNT2 displayed significantly increased metastatic ability, whereas treatment with an N-glycosylation inhibitor effectively suppressed this phenomenon. B3GNT2 promotes the trafficking of RYK to the plasma membrane of GC cells by mediating its N-glycosylation, thereby driving GC metastasis.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease

title: Spectral CT-based habitat analysis for predicting pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy in gastric cancer.
abstract: To investigate the predictive value of habitat imaging based on spectral CT-derived iodine maps (IMs) for pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) in gastric cancer (GC). This retrospective, two-center study included 151 patients with pathologically confirmed GC who underwent NAT followed by gastrectomy between July 2022 and June 2025. All patients underwent dual-phase, contrast-enhanced, dual-layer spectral CT scans before NAT. Based on tumor regression grade, patients were categorized as responders or non-responders. In venous-phase IMs, tumor voxels in the entire lesion were clustered into distinct habitats using the k-means algorithm. The volume fraction of each habitat and an intratumoral heterogeneity score (ITHscore) were calculated. Univariate analysis and logistic regression analyses determined predictive parameters among clinicopathologic and IM-based variables. A weighted logistic regression model for responders was developed and validated using fivefold cross-validation and an external test set. Among the 151 patients, 54 (35.8%) were responders. Three distinct perfusion habitats (high, middle, and low) were identified. Responders exhibited a higher volume fraction of the low-perfusion habitat and a lower ITHscore (both p < 0.05). By integrating these two metrics, patients were stratified into four perfusion subtypes, with response rates ranging from 75.0% to 17.4% (p < 0.001). The predictive model combining perfusion subtype and Lauren classification achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.794 (0.751-0.836) in internal cross-validation and 0.782 (0.605-0.909) in the external test set. IM-derived habitat imaging can distinguish distinct perfusion subtypes, suggesting a promising approach for predicting pathologic response to NAT in GC. Question Accurately predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant therapy prior to treatment in gastric cancer remains challenging due to the lack of reliable biomarkers. Findings Perfusion subtypes identified through iodine map-based habitat imaging effectively predict tumor regression in gastric cancer following neoadjuvant therapy. Clinical relevance Iodine map-based habitat imaging is a promising biomarker for noninvasively predicting pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy in patients with gastric cancer, thereby enabling more personalized treatment strategies for this population.

title: SENP1 drives glycolytic reprogramming to promote malignant progression of gastric cancer via deSUMOylation of HIF-1α.
abstract: Sentrin/SUMO-specific protease 1 (SENP1), a key deSUMOylating enzyme, stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) to promote tumor aerobic glycolysis. This study aims to determine whether SENP1 drives malignant progression in gastric cancer (GC) through glycolytic reprogramming. SENP1 and HIF-1α expression levels and their association with patient prognosis were analyzed using the GEPIA2.0 database. Clinical GC tissues were collected, and mRNA/protein expression levels were measured. SENP1 knockdown and overexpression models were established. Malignant phenotypes and glycolytic flux were assessed. SENP1-HIF-1α interaction and SUMOylation levels were determined. A subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was used for in vivo validation. SENP1 was upregulated in GC tissues and correlated with poor overall survival. SENP1 knockdown suppressed GC cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Conversely, SENP1 overexpression exerted opposing effects. Moreover, SENP1 depletion reduced glycolytic activity, as indicated by decreased glucose uptake, lactate release, ATP content, and expression of key glycolytic genes. Treatment with DMOG, which stabilizes HIF-1α, partially restored glycolytic activity and mitigated the malignant phenotypes driven by SENP1 knockdown. In vivo, SENP1 silencing impeded tumor growth and downregulated expression of HIF-1α, Ki-67, and key glycolytic genes. SENP1 may de‑SUMOylate HIF-1α, thereby driving glycolysis and malignant progression in GC cells. The SENP1‑HIF‑1α axis may play an important role in the metabolic reprogramming of GC, indicating that this axis could be a promising target for future metabolic interventions.

title: Consolidative Camrelizumab Following Definitive Concurrent Chemoradiation Therapy With Involved-Field Irradiation in Locally Advanced Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Arm Phase 2 Trial.
abstract: Definitive concurrent chemoradiation therapy (dCCRT) is considered the standard treatment for locally advanced unresectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). However, approximately half of the patients still experience local recurrence or distant metastasis. The CheckMate 577 trial, a phase III randomized clinical trial evaluating adjuvant nivolumab after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery, demonstrated that adjuvant nivolumab significantly improves disease-free survival in patients with resected esophageal or gastroesophageal junction cancer after neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy. However, the role of consolidation immunotherapy in locally advanced unresectable esophageal cancer remains unclear. Camrelizumab, an anti-programmed death receptor 1 antibody, has shown antitumor activity in advanced or metastatic ESCC. We conducted a clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy of camrelizumab consolidation therapy in patients with unresectable, locally advanced ESCC following dCCRT. This single-arm, phase 2 trial was conducted at the Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University (Shijiazhuang, China). Eligible patients were aged 18 to 75 years with histopathologically confirmed, locally advanced (T1bN+M0, T2-4N0-2M0, or supraclavicular lymph node metastasis) unresectable or medically inoperable ESCC, who had not experienced disease progression after completing dCCRT. Patients received camrelizumab consolidation therapy (200 mg intravenously, day 1, every 2 weeks) for 12 months. After 12 months, patients could independently choose to continue immunotherapy. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included disease control rate, objective response rate, duration of response, overall survival (OS), and safety. Between April 2020 and November 2023, 43 patients were screened, 35 were enrolled, and 32 were included in the analysis. As of the data cutoff date (July 25, 2025), 12 patients had experienced disease progression, and 10 patients had died. The disease control rate was 59.4% (19 of 32). Neither the median PFS nor the median OS was reached. The 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year PFS rates were 81.3%, 62.5%, and 62.5%, respectively. The 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year OS rates were 96.9%, 77.7%, and 63.0%, respectively. Regarding safety, most adverse events (AEs) were grade 1 or 2. The most common AEs were anemia (68.8%), leukopenia (50.0%), and reactive cutaneous capillary endothelial proliferation (43.8%). Grade 3 AEs included leukopenia (12.5%) and thrombocytopenia (3.1%). No treatment-related deaths occurred. The incidence of pneumonitis in the cohort was 31.3%; all cases were grade 1 or 2, with no grade ≥3 pneumonitis observed. Consolidation camrelizumab following dCCRT with involved-field irradiation demonstrates promising efficacy and manageable toxicity in patients with unresectable locally advanced ESCC.
journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics

title: Pretreatment multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT predicts tumor regression grade and survival in locally advanced gastric cancer.
abstract: Reliable pretreatment prediction of pathological response remains a major challenge in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). This study evaluated whether quantitative parameters from multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) can predict tumor regression grade (TRG) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) and provide prognostic information. We retrospectively analyzed 116 patients with cT2-4NxM0 gastric adenocarcinoma treated with NAC treatment followed by gastrectomy between January 2019 and December 2024. Quantitative imaging variables included phase-specific tumor attenuation ([Formula: see text], normalized enhancement difference ([Formula: see text]), normalized enhancement rate ([Formula: see text]), tumor area, and enhancement pattern. TRG was assessed on surgical specimens using the Mandard system; responders were defined as TRG 1-2 and non-responders as TRG 3-5. Candidate variables were screened by univariate analysis and Spearman correlation, then enrolled into weighted multivariable logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation. Associations with overall survival were evaluated using univariate Cox and Kaplan-Meier analyses. Forty-one patients were responders and 75 were non-responders. CA199, CEA, and age were independent clinical predictors. Among imaging features, venous-phase tumor attenuation ([Formula: see text]; OR = 8.809, 95% CI: 2.134-36.358, P = 0.003) and arterial-phase normalized enhancement rate ([Formula: see text]; OR = 3.200, 95% CI: 1.365-7.504, P = 0.007) independently predicted TRG response. The clinical, imaging, and combined models achieved mean AUCs of 0.746, 0.807, and 0.869, respectively; the combined model showed the best overall discrimination (accuracy 0.759, sensitivity 0.703, specificity 0.787) with good calibration. Higher [Formula: see text] (HR = 1.01, P = 0.004) and [Formula: see text] (HR = 1.01, P = 0.043) were associated with worse overall survival. Pretreatment CECT-derived quantitative features can predict TRG response in LAGC, and a combined clinical-imaging model improves predictive performance. Higher normalized enhancement rates in the venous and delayed phases are associated with poorer overall survival, supporting pre-treatment risk stratification in clinical practice.

title: IL-15 superagonists for reprogramming the immunosuppressive microenvironment in gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) adenocarcinomas pose a significant therapeutic challenge due to highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments that limit effective antitumor immune responses. Dense stromal fibrosis, immune exclusion and poor responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors are hallmarks of treatment-resistant malignancies, most notably pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and subsets of gastric cancer. In this regard, IL-15 superagonists such as N-803, NIZ985, RLI, and NKTR-255 have emerged as promising immunotherapeutic candidates, as they selectively expand natural killer (NK) cells and CD8+ T-cells without the systemic toxicity and regulatory T-cell activation observed with IL-2 therapy. IL-15 superagonists have emerged as more effective therapeutic agents when used in conjunction with local inhibitors of TGF-β and IL-10, stromal remodeling, and vascular normalization. They are supported by increasingly conclusive mechanistic, preclinical and early clinical data. A combination of these interventions circumvents extracellular matrix-provoked immune barriers, reverses VEGF-induced endothelial dysfunction, and enhances the trafficking of lymphocytes into tumor cores. Moreover, several localized therapeutic delivery strategies, such as endoscopic delivery, implantable depots, biomaterial scaffolds, and nanocarriers, can improve intratumoral cytokine retention and reduce systemic inflammatory toxicity. Together, these advances define a new paradigm for cytokine-immunotherapy: IL-15 superagonists serving as key mediators of reprogramming of the tumor microenvironment. Therapeutic strategies targeting IL-15 have the potential to restore cytotoxic immunity, improve access to immune cells, and promote responsiveness to the checkpoint blockade, making them a promising yet investigational approach to converting immune-cold GI malignancies into more treatment-responsive disease states, though further clinical validation is required.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of SOX9-CDK4 by CYD-4-61 impairs gastric adenocarcinoma growth and amplifies anti-PD-1 response.
abstract: Gastric adenocarcinoma (GAC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, particularly in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis, for whom effective therapies are limited. We investigated the therapeutic efficacy and molecular mechanism of CYD-4-61, a BAX activator, using human GAC cell lines, patient-derived xenograft models, genetically engineered mouse models, and a syngeneic mouse model. CYD-4-61 potently inhibited tumor cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and suppressed cancer stem cell-like properties, with enhanced activity in radiation-resistant GAC cells. Mechanistically, CYD-4-61 activated the BAX-caspase pathway, leading to SOX9 protein reduction. Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified SOX9-dependent transcriptional programs as major targets of CYD-4-61. Functional rescue experiments together with chromatin immunoprecipitation and CUT&RUN analyses supported CDK4 as a SOX9-regulated gene and demonstrated suppression of the SOX9-CDK4 regulatory axis following CYD-4-61 treatment. In multiple preclinical models, CYD-4-61 significantly inhibited tumor growth and improved the therapeutic response to anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy while modulating the tumor immune microenvironment. Clinically, co-expression of SOX9 and CDK4 was associated with diffuse-type GAC and poor patient outcomes. These findings identify the BAX-SOX9-CDK4 axis as an important mechanism contributing to the antitumor activity of CYD-4-61 and provide a strong preclinical rationale for its further development as a therapeutic strategy for aggressive GAC.

title: Alkalizer-based gastroretentive floating tablets of amoxicillin for localized gastric delivery.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori infection is a leading cause of peptic ulcer disease, yet amoxicillin trihydrate (AMX) efficacy is limited by its acid-catalyzed degradation and rapid gastric emptying. This study aimed to develop alkalizer-based gastroretentive floating tablets to enhance localized gastric-delivery and improve AMX stability under gastric conditions. Floating tablets were prepared by direct compression using HPMC K100M, sodium-bicarbonate and microcrystalline-cellulose. A 23 factorial-design (RStudio-v4.3.3) was used to optimize microenvironmental pH, floating lag time (FLT) and drug release. Optimized tablets were characterized for micromeritic properties, XRD, SEM, in vitro buoyancy, swelling, drug release, in vitro anti-H. pylori activity and in vivo gastric retention in Sprague-Dawley rats. The optimized formulation achieved a microenvironmental pH of 7.20 ± 0.26, FLT of 15.84 ± 0.50 s, and total floating time of approximately 12 h. Cumulative AMX release reached 98.49 ± 1.69% over 12 h with non-Fickian kinetics, and XRD/SEM analysis indicated reduced crystallinity and increased amorphous character of AMX within the hydrated matrix. The formulation showed significant in vitro anti-H. pylori activity and prolonged in vivo gastric retention. Alkalizer-based gastroretentive floating AMX tablets combined microenvironmental pH modulation with sustained gastric-retention, supporting their potential as a localized strategy for improved H. pylori eradication.

title: Prognostic value of circulating tumor DNA in esophageal and gastric cancer by treatment stage: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: The prognostic value of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) remains controversial. This meta-analysis systematically evaluates the association between ctDNA status and prognosis in esophageal cancer (EC) and gastric cancer (GC) (including gastroesophageal junction cancer), stratified by resectability and treatment stage. PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE and Scopus were systematically searched up to February 2026. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (95%CIs) were used to quantify disease-free survival (DFS), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Forty-four studies were included: 28 on resectable cancer, 17 on unresectable cancer (among which one study covered both types). In resectable cancer, ctDNA positivity was associated with worse DFS at baseline (HR=2.45, 95%CI: 1.18-5.07), after neoadjuvant therapy (HR=3.89, 95%CI: 2.50-6.06), after radical surgery (HR=6.76, 95%CI: 4.72-9.67), and follow-up (HR=19.17, 95%CI: 12.69-28.96). ctDNA positivity was also associated with worse OS at baseline (HR=1.89, 95%CI: 1.13-3.16), after neoadjuvant therapy (HR=3.40, 95%CI: 2.03-5.69), and after radical surgery (HR=4.52, 95%CI: 2.70-7.58). In resectable cancer, ctDNA positivity was associated with both DFS and OS, and the association differed between treatment time points (DFS: Q-test P<0.001; OS: Q-test P=0.05). In unresectable cancer, baseline ctDNA positivity was associated with worse PFS (HR=2.17, 95%CI: 1.31-3.60) and OS (HR=2.04, 95%CI: 1.54-2.70). During treatment, ctDNA positivity was associated with worse PFS (HR=2.72, 95%CI: 1.63-4.52) and OS (HR=2.63, 95%CI: 1.52-4.55). ctDNA positivity was associated with worse prognosis in both resectable and unresectable EC and GC. In resectable cancer, the association with DFS and OS differed between treatment time points.

title: Efficacy and safety of immunotherapy plus chemotherapy in elderly patients with advanced gastric cancer: a retrospective study.
abstract: This study investigated the efficacy and safety of immunotherapy plus chemotherapy in elderly patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative advanced gastric cancer (AGC). This single-center retrospective study included patients with HER2-negative AGC who received nivolumab or pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy between November 2021 and October 2025. Patients were classified as non-elderly (<75 years) or elderly (≥75 years). Endpoints included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and safety. A total of 164 patients were selected (117 non-elderly, 47 elderly). The median PFS was 6.4 and 7.4 months (Hazard Ratio (HR) 0.79; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.52-1.19), and median OS was 14.8 and 15.9 months (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.57-1.38). Initial dose reduction was significantly more frequent in elderly patients (35.9% vs. 83.0%, P < .001). Any grade AEs occurred in 97.4% and 97.9%, grade 3-4 AEs in 51.3% and 40.4%. Any grade immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in 31.6% and 27.7%, and grade 3-4 irAEs in 6.8% and 6.4% in non-elderly and elderly patients, respectively. Treatment discontinuation due to AEs was observed more frequent in the elderly group (3.4% vs. 17.0%). Fewer elderly patients received subsequent therapy (72.6% vs. 48.5%, P = .01). No clear age-related differences in survival outcomes or safety were observed with first-line immunotherapy plus chemotherapy in this study. However, elderly patients had higher treatment discontinuation and lower subsequent therapy rates, highlighting the importance of individualized dose adjustment and timely disease assessment and close monitoring.

title: Short-term surgical outcomes of robotic versus laparoscopic radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer: a propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Robotic gastrectomy (RG) is increasingly used for gastric cancer, but real-world comparative data from Chinese institutions during the early phase of robotic program implementation remain limited. We retrospectively identified patients who underwent radical gastrectomy between January 2015 and October 2025. The primary comparison included 54 patients who underwent RG and 162 who underwent Laparoscopic gastrectomy (LG). After exclusion of patients with missing propensity-score covariates, 53 RG and 143 LG patients were eligible for matching. One-to-two nearest-neighbor matching was performed using a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, yielding 45 RG and 88 LG patients. The principal outcomes was the number of lymph nodes retrieved. After matching, all included covariates were balanced. The median number of lymph nodes retrieved did not differ significantly between RG and LG (30 [interquartile range, 25-42] vs 34 [27-47]; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: -10.0-2.0, p = 0.181). RG was associated with a shorter postoperative length of stay (16 vs 18 days; 95% CI: -4.1-0.1, p = 0.016) and fewer positive lymph nodes (0 vs 2; 95% CI: -3.3-0.7, p = 0.007). Median operative time was 310 minutes for RG and 300 minutes for LG (95% CI: -20.5-40.5, p = 0.072). CUSUM analysis revealed a V-shaped recovery for LN retrieval, and confirmed operative efficiency convergence to the LG benchmark by the late phase (300 min, p = 0.053), together indicating a trend toward improved performance during the learning process. RG and LG achieved comparable lymph-node yields, while RG was associated with a shorter postoperative hospital stay. Exploratory sequential analyses suggested improvement in operative efficiency but did not establish a proficiency threshold. Complete outcome ascertainment and contemporaneous comparisons are needed.Clinical Trial: The study was registered retrospectively in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry on August 27, 2026 (ChiCTR2600131011; http://www.chictr.org.cn).

title: Vascular plasticity in the gastric cancer environment: mechanisms, prognostic significance, and concepts of therapeutic interventions.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global health problem because of its aggressive behavior and frequent development of therapeutic resistance. In GC, as in other malignancies, blood vessels are essential for Tumor-cell survival and dissemination, thereby facilitating metastasis to distant organs. As tumors grow, they remodel the surrounding microenvironment, generating hypoxic, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions with elevated interstitial fluid pressure. Reactive oxygen species further support tumor growth, glycolytic metabolism, and neovascularization. Highly aggressive cancer cells can also form endothelial cell-independent vascular-like networks defined as vasculogenic mimicry (VM), which may facilitate access to oxygen and nutrients. Many molecular markers and mechanisms underlying VM in GC remain insufficiently defined, while the presence of VM is associated with aggressive tumor behavior, metastatic potential, therapeutic resistance, and poor prognosis. Therefore, new therapeutic strategies are needed that complement conventional treatment and target the heterogeneous vascular compartments of GC. Nanomedicine may contribute to this goal by improving targeted drug delivery, local drug concentration, bioavailability, and controlled release while reducing systemic adverse effects.

title: Palliative radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis of bleeding response and dose-response relationships.
abstract: Palliative radiotherapy is commonly used to control bleeding in advanced gastric cancer; however, the optimal dose-fractionation regimen as well as the dose-response relationship remain unclear. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding and its association with dose fractionation. We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Ichushi-Web for studies published between January 2000 and August 2026 on palliative radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding. The primary endpoint was bleeding response rate. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate the pooled response rates. Meta-regression and subgroup analyses were conducted to explore dose-response relationships. Meta-regression was performed using study-level median biologically effective dose (BED) values. A total of 31 studies were included. The pooled bleeding response rate was 75.9% (95% confidence interval, 69.7-81.2), with significant heterogeneity (I2 = 67.5%). Egger's test suggested small study effects (P = 0.012). Meta-regression analysis demonstrated an association between a higher BED and an increased likelihood of response (P = 0.010). Subgroup analyses showed that higher BED categories were associated with higher response rates (P = 0.005). The pooled rebleeding rate was 32.4%. The median overall survival and rebleeding-free survival were 3.8 and 3.4 months, respectively. Radiotherapy was generally well tolerated, with a low incidence of grade ≥ 3 toxicities. Palliative radiotherapy is an effective and well-tolerated treatment for gastric cancer-related bleeding. Although study-level meta-regression identified a statistical association between higher BED and hemostatic response, this may largely reflect selection bias and methodological limitations rather than a true dose-response relationship. Given the poor prognosis of this population, shorter dose-fractionation regimens are appropriate for many patients, whereas higher-BED regimens remain reasonable for selected patients.

title: Identification of a novel Microbacterium species and biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles: activation of apoptosis and dysregulation of ABCG transporters in gastric adenocarcinoma cells.
abstract: Gastric cancer has high morbidity and mortality rates worldwide, often requiring new therapeutic approaches. Biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles (GNPs) offers a promising treatment due to their unique biological properties and biocompatibility. In this study, we synthesized gold nanoparticles using the cultural supernatant of Microbacterium sp. MAH-37 (MM37-S) and evaluated their anti-gastric cancer activity, focusing on apoptosis induction and regulation of the ABCG transporter pathway. The Microbacterium sp. strain MAH-37 was isolated from pumpkin garden soil, and its morphology was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The successful biosynthesis of MM37-S-GNP was confirmed by UV-visible spectroscopy, SAED, DLS, FTIR, XRD, EDX, and FE-TEM analyses. Biological evaluations revealed that MM37-S-GNPs exhibited cytotoxicity of approximately 72% at 200 µg/mL against AGS cells and confirmed by colony formation and Live/Dead assay, whereas normal HFE-145 cells was non-toxic. Furthermore, Hoechst 33,258, propidium iodide, and Mito Tracker revealed nuclear condensation and fragmentation, membrane-compromised cells, and mitochondrial disruption, respectively, indicating cell death via apoptosis. H2DCFDA staining demonstrated a significant increase intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in AGS cells following MM37-S-GNP. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that treatment induced apoptosis in AGS cells, with 30.4% apoptotic cells observed at 200 µg/mL. Consistently, mRNA and protein expression levels confirmed apoptosis cell death, as evidenced by an increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and elevated levels of cleaved caspase-9. Additionally, Western blot analysis revealed that treatment with higher doses of MM37-S-GNPs significantly downregulated the expression of ABCG1 and ABCG2 transporters. MM37-S-GNPs selectivelyeliminated gastric cancer cells through ROS-mediated mitochondrial damage and apoptotic pathways, while effectively regulating ABCG transporter expression, highlighting their potential as a promising nanotherapeutic agent.

title: Danshen Injection for 5-Fluorouracil-Resistant Gastric Cancer: Mitochondrial Apoptosis and Enhanced Drug Activity.
abstract: Gastric cancer ranks among the leading causes of cancer-related death worldwide, and the progressive emergence of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) resistance represents a critical barrier to the efficacy of conventional chemotherapy, particularly 5-FU-based regimens. Danshen injection (DI), a clinically approved intravenous preparation derived from Salvia miltiorrhiza, has demonstrated preliminary antineoplastic activity; however, the mechanistic basis underlying its reversal of 5-FU resistance in gastric cancer has not been systematically defined. This study aimed to evaluate the antitumor efficacy of DI and its potential for enhanced combined activity with 5-FU in human gastric cancer cell lines (SGC7901 and BGC823), their 5-FU-resistant variants, and a xenograft mouse model. DI significantly induced apoptosis in both parental and drug-resistant cell lines, while CCK-8 assays confirmed markedly elevated IC50 values in resistant variants, validating the chemoresistant phenotype. The combination of DI and 5-FU produced enhanced antitumor effects superior to either agent alone, as demonstrated by increased apoptotic rates, upregulated expression of cleaved PARP and cleaved caspase-3, impaired mitochondrial membrane potential by JC-10 assay, and reduced colony formation. Mechanistically, DI promoted cytochrome c translocation from mitochondria to the cytoplasm, and elevated cleaved caspase-9 levels, effects that were further amplified upon co-treatment with 5-FU. Consistent antitumor activity was validated in vivo, with the combination regimen demonstrating superior tumor suppression compared with monotherapy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that DI exerts meaningful antitumor activity and produces a greater combined effect with 5-FU in 5-FU-resistant gastric cancer. This study provides a preclinical rationale for incorporating DI into chemotherapy-based strategies for the management of 5-FU-resistant gastric cancer.

title: Dielectrophoresis-Assisted PVDF/DES/Au NP-Based Microfluidic ECL Biosensor for In Situ Detection of Extracellular Vesicles.
abstract: Herein, a regenerable dielectrophoresis (DEP)-assisted microfluidic electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensor was developed for in situ detection of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in gastric cancer ascites. In the integrated microfluidic ECL sensor, a poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP)/deep eutectic solvent (DES)/Au NP (PDES/Au NPs) self-supporting electrode was developed. The DES treatment increased the polar β-phase proportion in PVDF-HFP and improved its conductivity. Meanwhile, Au NPs deposited on the electrode surface amplified the ECL signal of Ru(bpy)32+/TPrA@SiO2 nanobeads through the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect and generated an inhomogeneous electric field distribution for EV capture. Due to the DEP effect, the polarized EVs migrated and enriched on the PDES/Au NP electrode surface. As a result, the isolation time of EVs was reduced from 120 to 30 min. Consequently, the sensing platform effectively captured and detected EVs in gastric cancer ascites. The detection range was 1.0 × 101.6-1.0 × 105.3 particles μL-1, and the limit of detection was 9 particles μL-1. Moreover, a regenerative strategy was designed by controllably cleaving Au-S bonds on the self-supporting electrode. This developed microfluidic ECL biosensor achieved real-time quantification of low-concentration EVs in ascites, which established a promising analytical tool for gastric cancer diagnosis as well as the discrimination of peritoneal metastatic lesions.

title: Integrated in silico and in vitro analysis identifies a co-expression pattern associated with cisplatin/5-FU treatment response and metastatic features in gastric cancer.
abstract: Gastric cancer remains a major cause of cancer mortality worldwide, and treatment failure is frequently associated with chemotherapy resistance and metastatic progression. Although cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil are commonly used components of gastric cancer chemotherapy, the extent to which gene-miRNA expression patterns associated with treatment response overlap with metastatic features remains incompletely understood. We integrated transcriptomic analysis of pretreatment GSE14210 samples with STRING network analysis and target-centric miRNA prioritization. Prioritized genes and miRNAs were evaluated by qRT-PCR in metastatic versus non-metastatic gastric cancer tissues and in MKN-45 3D spheroids exposed to cisplatin/5-FU; one patient-derived spheroid model was included as a feasibility observation. Analysis of the pretreatment GSE14210 cohort identified 414 upregulated DEGs, including 63 highly connected hubs (degree ≥ 10); 21 of these were also upregulated in tumor-versus-normal GEPIA comparisons. In metastatic tissues, CXCL8, MMP9, STAT1, miR-17-5p, miR-24-3p, and miR-124-3p were significantly increased, whereas miR-145-5p was significantly decreased; CCL5 was not significantly different. In cisplatin/5-FU-treated MKN-45 spheroids, CXCL8, MMP9, STAT1, miR-17-5p, miR-24-3p, and miR-124-3p showed significant expression changes, whereas CCL5 and miR-145-5p did not. MKN-45 spheroids regrew after cyclic exposure, consistent with an adaptive drug-tolerant phenotype, whereas the single patient-derived model showed limited recovery. These findings identify context-dependent candidate co-expression patterns across metastatic tissues and chemotherapy-exposed 3D models. They do not establish a shared causal mechanism and require functional validation in independent cohorts and additional patient-derived models.

title: Mechanistic insights into VSIR-mediated AXL regulation and gastric cancer proliferation.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) progression is frequently driven by complex tumor microenvironment signals. Here, our study identifies V-set immunoregulatory receptor (VSIR) as a key driver of GC progression via AXL regulation. High-throughput RNA sequencing demonstrated that VSIR overexpression potently induces AXL upregulation in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. This finding was confirmed through both VSIR overexpression and knockdown experiments. Mechanistically, our data demonstrated that STAT3 directly contributes to AXL transcriptional upregulation. Crucially, VSIR not only enhances LPS induced STAT3 phosphorylation, thereby amplifying AXL transcription, but also interacts with the AXL protein to stabilize it, leading to sustained AXL signaling. Functionally, the VSIR-AXL axis drives GC proliferation; notably, AXL inhibition suppresses this tumorigenesis, while combined AXL and HER2 blockade synergistically abrogates tumor growth. These findings reveal a critical oncogenic pathway and provide a strong rationale for dual-targeted therapeutic strategies in GC management.

title: Gastric and oesophageal cancer: ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up.
journal: Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology

title: Nivolumab-Ipilimumab for Localized Microsatellite Instability-High Gastric/Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma: The Phase 2 NEONIPIGA Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in localized deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma was evaluated in the NEONIPIGA study. The primary end point of pathological complete response (pCR) was previously reported. To report long-term follow-up results and secondary end points, including event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS), of the NEONIPIGA study. The NEONIPIGA study is a French, multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial that included patients with histologically proven cT2-T4NXM0 deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high GEJ adenocarcinoma who were eligible for surgery. Patients were enrolled between October 23, 2019, and June 4, 2021, and the database was locked on November 13, 2025. Neoadjuvant nivolumab, 240 mg, every 2 weeks for 6 cycles plus ipilimumab, 1 mg/kg, every 6 weeks for 2 cycles, followed by surgery 5 weeks after the last nivolumab dose, and adjuvant nivolumab, 480 mg, every 4 weeks for 9 cycles. EFS and OS. A total of 32 patients (median [range] age, 65 [40-80] years; 8 [28%] female and 21 [72%] were male) were included: 16 (50%) with gastric cancer and 16 (50%) with GEJ cancer. Three patients did not undergo surgery (1 with metastatic disease and 2 who refused). Twenty-seven patients (84%) completed neoadjuvant therapy and 14 (44%) received all treatment as planned. Neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 6 (19%) and 4 patients (17%), respectively. Median follow-up was 48.3 months (95% CI, 44.8-52.0 months). Among the 32 patients in the intention-to-treat population, 4-year OS was 84.1% (95% CI, 65.8%-93.0%). In the 31 patients eligible for surgery, 4-year EFS was 83.5% (95% CI, 64.8%-92.8%). One patient relapsed with cerebral metastases. Six deaths occurred: 2 related to gastric cancer or treatment (1 patient had postoperative complications and 1 cerebral metastases) and 4 unrelated. All patients who did not undergo surgery achieved a clinical complete response after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. One patient subsequently died of causes unrelated to their cancer. Overall, 17 of 29 patients (59%) achieved pCR on surgical specimen. Safety was previously reported, and no additional late toxic effects were observed. In this phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial, the immunotherapy regimen evaluated was associated with sustained long-term survival, but no clear evidence of improved survival over outcomes reported in other studies evaluating surgery alone in this patient population was observed. The high pCR rates and durable responses observed may provide useful information for designing future clinical studies, including randomized trials investigating organ-preserving strategies. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04006262.

title: Alteration of sublingual microcirculation in anemic patients during gastric cancer surgery under goal-directed fluid therapy: a prospective cohort study.
abstract: Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) relies primarily on macrocirculatory hemodynamic variables for optimizing fluid therapy. Patients undergoing gastric cancer surgery often present with anemia, which may impair microvascular endothelial function and tissue oxygenation. How preoperative anemia influences intraoperative sublingual microcirculation and macro- and micro-circulatory coherence under GDFT is not known. Patients undergoing open radical gastrectomy were divided into anemic and non‑anemic groups according to their hemoglobin (Hb) levels. All patients received GDFT guided by pulse pressure variation. Sublingual microcirculatory (microvascular flow index [MFI], proportion of perfused vessels [PPV], total and perfused vessel density) and macrocirculatory (cardiac index [CI] and mean arterial pressure [MAP]) variables were measured before (T0) and immediately after induction of general anesthesia (T1), after tumor resection (T2) and at the end of surgery (T3). Mixed linear models were used to compare intergroup differences in sublingual microcirculation over time, and to analyze the correlations between macro- and micro-circulatory variables. Correlations between preoperative Hb and changes in MFI from each intraoperative time point to T0 were additionally assessed. A total of 49 patients were analyzed in present study. MFI showed a significant group‑by‑time interaction between the two groups (P = 0.030). In anemic patients (n = 22), MFI was significantly lower than that in non‑anemic patients (n = 27) at T1 (P = 0.013), and between-group differences were no longer evident at T3 (P = 0.461) under GDFT, although MFI remained below baseline in both groups. PPV was lower in anemic patients at T2 (P = 0.010). Correlation analyses demonstrated that lower preoperative Hb levels were associated with greater reductions in ΔMFI from T1 to T0 (Pearson's r = 0.343, P = 0.016) and T2 to T0 (Spearman's ρ = 0.369, P = 0.009). No significant associations were found between macro- and micro-circulatory variables in either group. Under GDFT, anemic patients exhibited greater perioperative alterations in sublingual microcirculation, particularly after anesthesia induction and tumor resection. Lower preoperative Hb concentrations were associated with greater reductions in MFI. Further, the lack of detectable associations between macrocirculatory and sublingual microcirculatory variables suggests that conventional hemodynamic targets may not fully reflect sublingual microvascular perfusion in this vulnerable population.Trial registration number: NCT07583927.
journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing

title: Impact of AI-Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real-World Study.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions. Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77). AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.

title: Dynamic changes of claudin 18.2 expression after systemic therapy in gastric and esophagogastric junction cancer.
abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a promising therapeutic target in gastric/esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma (GC/EGJC), but its dynamic expression during systemic therapy is unclear. CLDN18.2 expression by immunohistochemistry in paired tumor samples from 155 patients with advanced GC/EGJC was retrospectively evaluated before and after systemic therapy. CLDN18.2-positive was defined as ≥75% of viable tumor cells exhibiting moderate-to-strong (2+ or 3+) membranous staining. Among all patients, 54 (34.84%) were CLDN18.2-positive. Following treatment, the proportion of CLDN18.2-positive patients increased significantly to 61 (39.35%) (p < .001). Among patients who were CLDN18.2-negative at baseline, 57 (56.44%) showed increased expression after treatment, including 22 (21.78%) who converted to positive status. In contrast, among those CLDN18.2-positive at baseline, expression decreased in 35 patients (64.81%), with 15 (27.78%) converting to negative status (p < .001). Among patients receiving chemotherapy alone (n = 25), 1 (4.00%) converted to negative and 5 (20.00%) converted to positive, whereas among those receiving chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy (n = 130), 14 (10.77%) converted to negative and 17 (13.08%) converted to positive (p = .45). A total of 131 patients (84.52%) demonstrated changes in CLDN18.2 expression following therapy, encompassing both conversions across the positivity threshold and fluctuations within the same classification. CLDN18.2 expression in GC/EGJC is dynamic and frequently altered after systemic therapy. These findings support reassessment of CLDN18.2 status before initiating CLDN18.2-targeted therapies.

title: Methylmalonic Acid Induces Oxaliplatin Resistance Through Promoting DNA Damage Repair via the ATM/ATR Pathway in Gastric Cancer.
abstract: Surgical intervention and chemotherapy have enhanced the survival rates of patients with advanced gastric cancer. However, the development of chemotherapy resistance remains a major obstacle to effective treatment, leading to poor prognosis in these patients. Increasing evidence suggests that metabolic alterations play crucial roles in mediating chemoresistance. Here we investigate the effects of methylmalonic acid (MMA), a mitochondrial-derived metabolite, on GC progression and oxaliplatin resistance. Analysis of clinical samples revealed that elevated serum MMA levels correlated with chemoresistance and advanced tumor stage in GC patients. Functional assays identified that MMA promoted GC cell proliferation, migration, and resistance to oxaliplatin by attenuating DNA damage. Mechanistically, MMA suppressed oxaliplatin-induced γH2AX expression while upregulating ATAD5 and activating the ATM/ATR-mediated homologous recombination (HR) repair pathway. In vivo studies further confirmed that MMA impaired the antitumor efficacy of oxaliplatin, while silencing PCCA, a key enzyme in MMA synthesis, or supplementing vitamin B12, a regulator of MMA metabolism, reversed MMA-induced chemoresistance. These findings highlight MMA as a potential indicator for oxaliplatin resistance and a therapeutic target in GC. Therefore, targeting MMA through vitamin B12 supplementation could serve as a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in GC patients with elevated MMA levels.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

title: Solasonine inhibits growth of gastric cancer by targeting FTL-mediated ferroptosis.
abstract: Solasonine (SS), a principal bioactive constituent of Solanum nigrum L., has attracted considerable attention due to its pronounced cytotoxic effects on cancer cells. Nevertheless, the precise mechanism of SS against gastric cancer remains inadequately explored. In this study, the therapeutic effects and potential targets of SS against gastric cancer were investigated. The results showed that SS markedly inhibited cell proliferation and promoted cell death in gastric cancer cells. Pharmacological inhibition studies revealed that the antitumor effects of SS predominantly rely on ferroptosis rather than apoptosis, necroptosis, or autophagy. This was corroborated by dysregulation of ferroptosis-related molecular markers, increased intracellular lipid peroxidation (LPO), malondialdehyde (MDA), and Fe2+ levels, and depletion of glutathione (GSH). Proteomic profiling identified ferritin light chain (FTL) as a putative target of SS, which was further supported by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and western blot. Bioinformatics analyses demonstrated that FTL expression is significantly elevated at both the mRNA and protein levels in gastric cancer tissues. Higher FTL expression correlates with poorer overall survival. Overexpression of FTL in gastric cancer cells promoted the proliferation and mitigated SS-induced ferroptosis. In mice, SS treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth, suppressed FTL protein expression, and induced ferroptosis in gastric cancer xenografts. And the above effects can be rescued by application of a ferroptosis inhibitor. The antitumor activity and ferroptosis induction by SS were further validated using human organoid models. These findings demonstrate that SS inhibits gastric cancer growth by direct binding to FTL and promoting FTL-mediated ferroptosis. This mechanistic insight underscores the clinical applicability of SS for gastric cancer treatment.

title: Th1-biased iNKT cell agonist-loaded liposomal peptide vaccines synergize with a PD-L1 inhibitor to boost immunotherapy against gastric cancer.
abstract: We covalently conjugated the Th epitope DT331-345 with the MG3 peptide and co-encapsulated the conjugate with an iNKT cell agonist into liposomes to prepare a vaccine. The DT-MG3/GCS-11 formulation elicited strong antibody responses and promoted T-cell responses. Notably, its combination with PD-L1 inhibitor BMS-202 suppressed tumor growth and prolonged the survival in tumor-bearing mice.

title: Tumor NLRP3 amplification promotes immunotherapy resistance by inhibiting STAT1 signaling and MHC class I expression.
abstract: Immunotherapy resistance remains a challenge in immuno-oncology, and predictive biomarkers are needed to guide combination immunotherapy selection for the individual patient. We showed that elevated tumor-intrinsic NOD-, LRR-, and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) signaling activity correlates with checkpoint inhibitor resistance in several independent cohorts of stage III/IV melanoma and gastroesophageal (GE) adenocarcinoma. In situ hybridization demonstrated tumor NLRP3 copy number gain in immunotherapy-resistant melanomas and GE adenocarcinomas harboring enhanced NLRP3 signaling activity. Nlrp3 amplification suppressed NOD-, LRR-, and CARD-containing 5-mediated (NLRC5-mediated) MHC class I upregulation, while spatial transcriptomic analysis of patient-derived GE adenocarcinomas confirmed that NLRP3 signaling activity inversely correlated with NLRC5 and MHC class I-associated gene expression. Mechanistically, NLRP3 binds to and inhibits signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) dimerization, nuclear translocation, and NLRC5 transcription. Consistent with these findings, pharmacologic inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome augmented tumor STAT1/NLRC5 signaling, enhanced MHC class I surface expression, and overcame anti-programmed cell death 1 resistance in an orthotopic model of gastric adenocarcinoma. This work reveals a fundamental link between cellular stress and tumor-mediated immune evasion and indicates that the tumor NLRP3 signaling pathway merits further clinical study as a therapeutic target and a source of companion biomarkers for overcoming checkpoint inhibitor resistance in patients with cancer.

title: Tumor empowered binary macrophages regulate T cell interferon signaling to mediate immunotherapy resistance in gastric cancer.
LC-MS/MS-Based Phytochemical Characterization of Cakile maritima Methanol Extract and Its Photodynamic Anticancer Activity in Gastric Cancer Cells.
abstract: In this study, the phytochemical composition, in vitro anticancer activity, photodynamic therapy (PDT) activity, and molecular interaction potential with carbonic anhydrase IX (CA IX) of Cakile maritima methanol extract were evaluated. LC-MS/MS analysis identified 11 compounds among 35 screened phytochemicals, with fumaric acid (13797.19 ppb), ferulic acid (771.37 ppb) and p-coumaric acid (601.95 ppb) accounting for approximately 97% of the total content. Molecular docking results demonstrated that sinapic acid (-6.13 kcal/mol) and quinic acid (-6.11 kcal/mol) exhibited the highest binding affinities toward CA IX. Cell culture studies revealed that LogIC50 values differed significantly among cell lines (p < 0.0001). PDT applied to the MKN-28 gastric cancer cell line significantly enhanced cytotoxicity compared with the control group, with the highest photodynamic efficacy observed under green-light irradiation (p < 0.0001). These findings indicate that C. maritima methanol extract exhibits light-enhanced cytotoxicity in MKN-28 gastric cancer cells and warrant further investigation regarding its potential photosensitising properties.
journal: Rapid communications in mass spectrometry : RCM

title: Development and validation of an explainable model for predicting lymph node metastasis in early gastric cancer: a multicenter retrospective study with external and prospective validation.
abstract: Accurate preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is essential for treatment selection in early gastric cancer (EGC), particularly when considering endoscopic submucosal dissection. Existing approaches show limited sensitivity for metastatic disease and frequently lack external or prospective validation. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model for individualized preoperative prediction of LNM in EGC. In this multicenter study, four cohorts from three tertiary centers were included. Patients with pathologically confirmed EGC who underwent gastrectomy with lymph node dissection were retrospectively enrolled for training and external validation. A temporally independent cohort (September 2023-December 2024) was prospectively enrolled for validation. A preoperative pathology validation cohort (January 2025-January 2026) was also analyzed. Clinicopathological variables were selected using LASSO regression. SMOTE was applied to address class imbalance. Six machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was assessed using AUC and PR-AUC, and interpretability was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations. A web-based calculator was developed. Among 3412 patients in the training cohort, 467 (13.7%) had LNM. XGBoost achieved the best discrimination (training AUC = 0.9289) and maintained robust performance in the external (AUC = 0.8583; PR-AUC = 0.6079) and prospective validation cohorts (AUC = 0.8766; PR-AUC = 0.5137). In the preoperative pathology validation cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.8653 and a PR-AUC of 0.6050. Key predictors included lymphovascular/neural invasion, invasion depth, tumor location, differentiation, and tumor size. This externally and prospectively validated, interpretable machine-learning model provides transparent individualized risk estimates and may support personalized decision-making between endoscopic and surgical management in EGC.
journal: European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical Oncology

title: An integrated pathological-radiological downstaging score for prognostic classification in gastric cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy: A multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) followed by surgery is the standard treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). However, post-therapy staging based on ypTNM mainly reflects residual pathological status and does not capture pretreatment disease burden or the extent of tumor regression after NAC, limiting postoperative prognostic stratification. To address this limitation, we developed a Pathological-Radiological Integrated Model (PRIM) that combines baseline stage, post-treatment pathology, and radiologic response. We enrolled 414 patients with LAGC who underwent radical gastrectomy after NAC, including 348 in a development cohort and 66 in an external validation cohort. A Down-stage System (DS) was constructed to quantify tumor stage changes after NAC by weighting cT/cN and ypT/ypN categories using multivariable Cox regression. DS was then combined with RECIST response to establish the PRIM system. Prognostic performance and clinical utility were evaluated and compared with conventional ypTNM staging. PRIM stratified patients into four distinct risk groups with significantly different 3-year overall survival rates (86.9%, 69.9%, 40.0%, 21.2%; P < 0.001). Compared with ypTNM, PRIM demonstrated improved prognostic performance, with a higher C-index (0.728 vs. 0.696, P < 0.001), AUC (0.775 vs. 0.731, P < 0.001), and better model fit (AIC: 1471.62 vs. 1509.33; BIC: 1474.61 vs. 1512.32). Risk reclassification was also improved (NRI 14.49%; IDI 8.9%). Time-dependent ROC analysis showed consistently higher predictive accuracy for PRIM over 5 years. By integrating pathological and radiological response information, the PRIM classification provides improved postoperative prognostic stratification compared with ypTNM alone in patients with LAGC treated with NAC.
journal: European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical Oncology

title: Metal-Center-Controlled Fenton-Like Reactivity of Biomimetic First-Row Transition Metal Complexes in Aqueous Anticancer Catalysis.
abstract: Catalytic oxidative cancer therapy exploits elevated hydrogen peroxide levels within tumor microenvironments to induce selective oxidative damage in malignant cells. However, many ROS-generating therapeutic systems rely on heavy metals or structurally complex inorganic architectures, limiting their biological compatibility and catalytic selectivity. Inspired by nonheme iron-mediated redox catalysis, we report a series of water-soluble biomimetic first-row transition metal complexes supported by a picolylamine-derived nonheme ligand scaffold bearing a pendant hydroxyl group. Systematic variation of the metal center (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) generated divergent electrochemical behavior and distinct peroxide-activation reactivity, yet only the iron complex, [Fe(N2Py3OH)]2+ (1-Fe), promoted hydroxyl radical formation via Fenton-like hydrogen peroxide activation in water. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and crystallographic analyses revealed a biomimetic coordination environment that stabilizes a quasi-reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) redox couple suited to catalytic peroxide activation. In gastric cancer cells, 1-Fe induced intracellular oxidative stress, mitochondrial depolarization, lipid peroxidation, and concomitant apoptosis and ferroptosis, while exhibiting negligible toxicity toward normal fibroblasts. In combination with paclitaxel, 1-Fe produced synergistic antiproliferative activity in vitro and suppressed peritoneal tumor dissemination in vivo without overt systemic toxicity. Collectively, these results establish biomimetic iron complexes as molecular platforms for Fenton-like oxidative catalysis in redox-based cancer therapy.

title: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.

title: A microbial chromatin remodeler drives gastric cancer progression and immune evasion by reprogramming the host epigenome.
abstract: First-line treatment for gastric cancer (GC) includes PD-1 blockade with chemotherapy, but resistance challenges treatment success. We identify Streptococcus anginosus (SA) as a tumor-resident oncobacterium driving GC progression and immune evasion. SA is enriched in GC patient tumors and drives tumor growth in mice. SA extracellular vesicles (saEVs) translocate the bacterial chromatin remodeler saSNF2 into host cells. saSNF2 partners with host transcription factor TEAD1-through its ATPase activity and participation in BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complex assembly-to activate oncogenic transcription. This transkingdom interaction upregulates the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC11, which stabilizes PD-L1 via palmitoylation to establish an immunosuppressive niche, while amplifying other TEAD1 target genes to fuel tumor progression. saEVs promote tumor growth and limit CD8+ T cell infiltration in vivo. Pharmacological inhibition of ZDHHC11 reverses immune evasion and synergizes with anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade. These findings establish SA as a multifaceted driver of GC and highlight the saSNF2-ZDHHC11 axis as a target to potentiate immunotherapy.

title: Postoperative malnutrition predicts severe chemotherapy toxicity after gastrectomy: evaluation of an inflammation-anemia phenotype.
abstract: Severe toxicity during adjuvant chemotherapy after curative gastrectomy is common. We evaluated whether postoperative malnutrition predicts severe toxicity, whether an inflammation-anemia (IA) composite adds incremental information, and whether a simple risk model offers clinical utility. In this single-center prospective cohort, adults received adjuvant chemotherapy after curative gastrectomy. Malnutrition was defined as albumin <35 g/L, BMI <18.5 kg/m2, or low skeletal muscle index; IA as CRP ≥1.5 mg/L plus hemoglobin <120 g/L. A ridge-penalized logistic model included age, pathologic stage, regimen (S-1 vs. oxaliplatin-based multi-agent), malnutrition, IA, and a malnutrition × regimen interaction. Nested 5-fold cross-validation and decision curve analysis evaluated model performance and net benefit. Of 222 screened patients, 219 were analyzed. Severe toxicity occurred in 48/219 (21.9 %), more often with multi-agent therapy than S-1 (23.5 vs. 8.7 %). Malnutrition was strongly associated with toxicity and remained an independent predictor (penalized OR 3.42, 95 % CI 1.75-6.68), whereas IA was not. Out-of-sample AUROC was 0.695, Brier score 0.156, and calibration slope 0.86. At a 0.30 threshold, net benefit was higher for the full model than for base + malnutrition. Postoperative malnutrition is a key predictor of severe adjuvant chemotherapy toxicity after gastrectomy. This parsimonious model may support risk-adapted supportive care and treatment planning.

title: Early detection of gastric cancer using DNA features in red blood cells, with multicenter validation.
abstract: Early detection of gastric cancer (GC) is limited by invasive endoscopy and poor sensitivity of blood-based biomarkers. Red blood cells (RBCs), the most abundant cells in the circulation, are anucleate but can retain DNA remnants that have been associated with pathological stress. Here, we report a non-invasive strategy for GC detection based on genome-wide profiling of DNA remnants retained in RBCs (rbcDNA). We performed shallow whole-genome sequencing of rbcDNA from 1-2 mL of peripheral blood of 865 individuals, including 434 treatment-naive GC patients and 431 non-GC controls with benign gastric conditions. In the discovery cohort, we identified 1,000 reproducible rbcDNA read-depth features distinguishing GC from non-cancer states. A machine learning classifier based on dimensionally reduced GC-associated rbcDNA features was trained in the discovery cohort (n = 435), with the cutoff fixed at 90% specificity, and evaluated in a test cohort (n = 109) and three independent multicenter validation cohorts (n = 321). The classifier achieved the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 84% in nested cross-validation of the discovery cohort and 95% in the test cohort. Across three hospital-based multicenter validation cohorts, performance remained consistent, with 83%-90% overall sensitivity and 82%-89% sensitivity for stage I GC. Additionally, the classifier distinguished early-stage GC from precancerous lesions and other tumors and detected ∼80% of GC cases negative for tumor markers. These findings demonstrate the potential of rbcDNA as a non-invasive biomarker for early-stage GC detection. This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Program of Zhejiang Province (2026C02A1176 and 2024C03170).

title: Patient-derived gastric cancer organoids for functional precision oncology: disease-specific bottlenecks and clinical readiness.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) poses a distinct modeling challenge. The disease varies by region, histology, metastatic site, and treatment history. It also develops within a gastric niche shaped by acid, mucus, polarity, microbes, and stroma. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) can preserve tumor-linked epithelial states and support living biobanks. They also enable genotype-phenotype studies and functional testing of therapeutic vulnerabilities. Their clinical value depends on representation, not model complexity alone. The assay must also return clear results within a useful clinical window. This review evaluates GC PDOs as functional companion models for precision oncology rather than stand-alone treatment decision tools. We discuss four barriers that limit clinical readiness. Establishment bias reduces representation of diffuse-type, scirrhous, and signet-ring cell carcinomas. Standard organoid lumens do not reproduce gastric acidity, stratified mucus, or Helicobacter pylori-driven polarity loss. Long-term expansion can select culture-adapted clones and weaken clinical representativeness. PDO drug screening also remains difficult to align with urgent treatment timelines. Fresh-sample assays may shorten turnaround time but reduce scale and depth. We further highlight biological insights gained from GC organoids. These include niche independence, epigenetic dependencies, ARID1A-linked vulnerabilities, and chemotherapy resistance. We propose a readiness framework based on six criteria: tumor authenticity, subtype coverage, niche fidelity, turnaround time, assay standards, and outcome validation. This framework may help define where GC PDOs can support clinical reasoning.

title: CAD potentially mediates 5‑fluorouracil resistance in gastric cancer cells via modulation of uridine monophosphate synthetase expression.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a malignant tumor originating from the gastric mucosal epithelium. While chemotherapy shows initial efficacy in early treatment, it often leads to tumor drug resistance. Studies indicate that over 90% of cancer patient deaths are associated with chemotherapy resistance. Based on this, we explored the expression significance of the pyrimidine metabolism gene CAD in GC. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that CAD expression correlates with survival duration, clinical characteristics, and the prognosis in GC patients. Drug sensitivity analysis revealed an association between CAD and 5-fluorouracil. Experimental validation demonstrated that CAD expression influences GC cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis, with this phenomenon also observed in drug-resistant cells. CAD exhibits positive correlation and co-expression with UMPS. This study confirms the high expression of CAD in GC cells, which may promote malignant phenotype transformation through its interaction with UMPS.

title: [Multimodal treatment of locally advanced and oligometastatic esophageal cancer].
abstract: Esophageal cancer is one of the most striking examples of the success of multimodal treatment concepts in gastrointestinal oncology. For locally advanced, resectable adenocarcinoma, perioperative chemotherapy with the FLOT regimen has replaced neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy according to CROSS following the ESOPEC trial and represents the current standard, whereas for squamous cell carcinoma neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery remains established. Immunotherapy is expanding the treatment spectrum: adjuvant nivolumab is established for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CheckMate-577); perioperative durvalumab combined with FLOT improves event-free survival in gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer (MATTERHORN). The SANO trial demonstrated noninferiority of active surveillance versus standard esophagectomy with respect to 2‑year overall survival in clinical complete responders; however, a decision analytical model based on the SANO data published in 2026 suggests potential long-term advantages of standard resection. In oligometastatic disease, FLOT5/RENAISSANCE showed no overall survival benefit for supplementary surgical resection and in this situation patient selection remains the central challenge. Future strategies will concentrate more on biological criteria, with a more precise definition of oligometastatic constellations, integrated immunotherapy and emerging biomarkers such as circulating tumor DNA.

title: EpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics regulate nuclear deformation and promote gastric cancer metastasis.
abstract: Diffuse gastric cancer is highly metastatic and lacks effective therapeutic targets. Using membrane proteomics, gastric cancer cell models, biophysical measurements, and in vivo metastasis assays, we identify EpCAM as a regulator of membrane-cytoskeletal mechanics. EpCAM overexpression was associated with reduced apparent plasma membrane tension, ERM-actin remodeling, increased traction forces, and nuclear deformation. Functional perturbation of ezrin and lamin A/C supported the involvement of membrane-cytoskeleton-nucleus mechanical coupling in confined migration. EpCAM knockout or monoclonal antibody blockade reduced tumor invasion and lymph node dissemination in vivo. These findings establish a mechanobiological framework linking EpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics to metastatic behavior and highlight EpCAM-associated mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in diffuse gastric cancer.

title: Association Between Neoadjuvant Immunochemotherapy Efficacy and Pathologic Characteristics in dMMR Gastric/Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NAIC) is feasible and associated with a high rate of pathologic complete response (pCR) in deficient mismatch repair (dMMR)/microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers (GC/GEJC). However, the association between NAIC efficacy and pathologic characteristics remains unclear. We conducted a retrospective study to evaluate this relationship. Patients with dMMR/MSI-H GC/GEJC who received neoadjuvant immunotherapy were included.
